# The Vacant Lot

Beside one of the holiest buildings in Japan there is a rectangle of white gravel, roughly the same size, and in a sense it is the holier of the two. In the middle of the gravel sits a small hut, and inside the hut is a wooden post, and the post is not much to look at. Tourists photograph the shrine — the cypress columns, the thatched roof with its ridge like a folded book, the crossed finials stabbing at the sky. Almost nobody photographs the gravel. But the gravel is the part I keep thinking about.

Every twenty years, the shrine at Ise is taken apart and built again on the empty plot next door. The old one is dismantled, its timbers dispersed to other shrines around the country or buried or given away, and the vacant lot becomes the shrine and the shrine becomes the vacant lot. Then the post is moved, and the hut, and the twenty years start over. The most recent rebuilding was in 2013, the sixty-second. The next is scheduled for 2033. The first is said to have been in 690.

I say "said to" because the record is not clean. There was a gap of something like a hundred and twenty years in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, when the country was at war with itself and the money and the peace both ran out. The cycle lapsed and then was picked back up. So even the paradigm case of unbroken tradition has a fracture in it, a place where the thing stopped and had to be restarted by people who had never seen it done. I find this more moving than a clean line would be. An unbroken chain is just a fact. A chain that broke and was re-forged from memory is an achievement.

The obvious question is which building is the shrine. This is the Ship of Theseus, which Plutarch reports the philosophers arguing about: the ship kept in the harbor, planks replaced as they rotted, until the Athenians could not agree whether it was still the same ship. Hobbes sharpened it nastily — suppose someone collected all the discarded planks in a warehouse and reassembled them. Now which one is the ship? The one with continuous history and no original matter, or the one with all the original matter and a gap in its history?

At Ise they have simply declined the dilemma, or rather they have answered it so decisively that the question doesn't arise. It's the new one. It's the new one because it's the new one that the rites are performed at, and the rites are the point. The gravel plot is not a construction site. It is a shrine in the interval between manifestations.

---

The European answer, historically, went the other way, and it went there hard. For a certain nineteenth-century sensibility, authenticity lived in the substance. The stones were the thing. Ruskin, in *The Seven Lamps of Architecture*, called restoration "the most total destruction which a building can suffer" — worse than ruin, because ruin is at least honest, while restoration gives you a forgery and tells you it's your inheritance. Let the building die, he said, and die with dignity; take care of it, count the old stones as an old man counts his years, and when it goes, let it go.

Against him, Viollet-le-Duc, who restored half of medieval France and defined restoration as re-establishing a building in a complete state that may never have existed at any moment. He wasn't lying about it, either. He thought the building had an intention, a logic, and that the logic was the real artifact; if the west front was never finished, finishing it was fidelity, not falsification. He was, in his way, closer to Ise than to Ruskin. He believed the thing being preserved was a design rather than a deposit.

But practice has always been messier than the theory. When the campanile of San Marco fell down in 1902 — simply fell, into a heap, in the middle of Venice — the Venetians rebuilt it and reopened it in 1912, "where it was and as it was," and nobody now thinks of it as a fake, though it is ten years old in a city that measures itself in millennia. When Warsaw's old town was deliberately dynamited, the Poles rebuilt it from rubble and from eighteenth-century paintings by Bellotto, who had rendered the streets so precisely that his canvases functioned as architectural survey drawings. Paintings became blueprints. UNESCO listed the reconstruction in 1980 precisely *as* a reconstruction, an outstanding example of it. The Frauenkirche in Dresden lay in a pile of blackened sandstone for forty-five years as a war memorial, and then thousands of those stones were catalogued and sorted and put back into a new building in their old positions, so that the reconstructed church is pale and freckled with dark, a new thing with the old scars distributed through it like a birthmark. Mies van der Rohe's Barcelona Pavilion stood for eight months in 1929, was taken down, and was rebuilt in the 1980s from photographs; the version you can visit is the third-hand one and it is not considered a lesser object.

So the West has its Ise cases too. What it lacked until recently was a doctrine that admitted them. That arrived in 1994, in Nara, at a conference on authenticity where the Japanese hosts made the point that a criteria of heritage built entirely around original material would disqualify their most important monument. The resulting document widened the field: authenticity could reside in form and design, in use and function, in traditions and techniques, in spirit and feeling. It is one of those rare bureaucratic texts that actually changed what a word means.

---

But the reason I keep returning to the gravel is not the metaphysics. It's the engineering, in a sense that has nothing to do with wood.

Twenty years is a strange interval for a building. It's too short to be about maintenance — the shrine could plainly last longer; thatched roofs need work but not total replacement on a fixed clock, and the untreated cypress would stand for a good while. The commonly offered explanation is that twenty years is the length of a generation of hands. A man who watches the rebuilding as an apprentice of twenty will direct it at forty and oversee it as an elder at sixty. Three times, if he lives long. Any longer and the knowledge has to survive a gap, and knowledge does not survive gaps.

Because that is the actual thing being conserved. Not a building. A capacity. The carpentry, obviously, but also the thatching, and the growing of the miscanthus that the thatch is made from, and the cutting of the cypress, and the metalwork, and the weaving and dyeing of the cloth, and the salt and the sake and the pottery for the offerings, and the songs, and the sequence of the rites, and the several hundred sacred treasures — many of which are replicas of objects whose originals were lost centuries ago, copies of copies, and some of which no living person has ever seen because they are kept wrapped and are simply remade, faithfully, by someone who was told how.

You cannot store any of that in an archive. You can store *descriptions* of it in an archive, which is a different thing, the way a recipe is a different thing from a cook. Michael Polanyi's line — we can know more than we can tell — is nowhere more literally true than in a craft. George Sturt, a wheelwright who inherited a shop in Surrey and wrote a book about it in 1923, tried to write down what his men knew and found he couldn't. The dish of a wheel, the slight cone that makes it survive the sideways lurch of a cart on a rutted road, was determined by feel, by a judgment passed from hand to hand, adjusted for each cart and each road, and none of the men could have stated the rule because there wasn't one. There was a competence. It lived in them, and it went into the ground with them.

So Ise is a machine for forcing a transmission. It's a curriculum with a building at the end of it. The twenty-year clock means the knowledge can never be merely theoretical for longer than a couple of decades; every generation is compelled to actually do the thing, at full scale, with real consequences for failure, in front of witnesses. The empty lot is a calendar. It says: *someone is going to have to know how to do this, and soon, and it might as well be you.*

Once you see it this way, a lot of things rearrange.

---

The two failure modes become clear, and they are opposites.

The first is matter without technique. The Rosetta Stone survived beautifully; granite is patient. What did not survive was anyone who could read it. The last hieroglyphic inscription anyone carved was in the fourth century; by the time Champollion cracked it in 1822, the writing had been mute for something like fourteen hundred years. The stone was perfectly preserved and completely useless, an object of enormous durability and zero legibility, and it took an accident of bureaucratic multilingualism to make it speak again. The Antikythera mechanism sat on the seafloor for two thousand years with its gears intact and its purpose gone; we only began to read its inscriptions properly in the 2000s with X-ray tomography, and even now, having read them, we cannot make another one. Roman concrete outlasts ours in seawater and we have only recently begun to argue convincingly about why — something about hot mixing and lime clasts that let the material heal its own cracks. Wootz steel had a carbide structure that smiths produced for centuries without knowing they were exploiting trace vanadium in particular ore bodies; when the ore changed, the technique died, and the death was invisible because nobody knew what the technique had depended on.

The most humiliating version is recent. In 1986 the BBC made a new Domesday Book, a survey of Britain on interactive laserdisc, a marvel, deliberately timed to the nine-hundredth anniversary of the original. Within about fifteen years it was essentially unreadable — the players were gone, the formats orphaned, the software stranded. The 1086 Domesday Book, written on animal skin with iron gall ink, remains readable by anyone who learns the Latin. We keep worrying about bit rot, which is the wrong worry. Bits are easy to copy perfectly and forever. What rots is the surrounding apparatus of understanding, the thing that makes a copy mean anything.

The second failure mode is the mirror image: technique without matter, and this one, it turns out, is not a failure mode at all. It's how most of the durable things in the world actually work.

A sourdough starter is a lineage. Every feeding discards most of what was there and replaces it with new flour and water; the substance is entirely turned over on a scale of days. People boast about hundred-year-old starters and are, in a sense, right, though nothing in the jar is older than lunch. What persists is a population and a practice — an ecosystem kept alive by being continually fed and continually thrown away. Latin is the same. Latin did not die; it was copied badly, by children, for a thousand years, in every valley slightly differently, and the accumulated errors became French and Spanish and Romanian. A language survives by being transmitted imperfectly. Sanskrit took the opposite route: Pāṇini's grammar froze it, fixed it so precisely that it could be transmitted without drift, and it worked — and what you get is a language of extraordinary preservation that stopped being anybody's mother tongue. Fixed things are stable. Living things are stable *and* adaptive, at the cost of never being quite the same.

---

You are, of course, one of these. The comfortable version of this observation is that your atoms turn over and you're a river, not a stone, a pattern persisting through matter in flux. It's true enough as far as it goes. Gut lining replaces itself in days; red cells last about four months; fat cells hang around roughly a decade; the skeleton remakes itself on a similar order. The "every seven years" figure people quote is folk numerology.

The real picture is stranger, and we know it because of an accident of the Cold War. Atmospheric nuclear testing nearly doubled the carbon-14 in the air and then, after the test ban, it declined in a clean curve. Anything built from atmospheric carbon since 1955 carries a date stamp. Jonas Frisén's group in Stockholm used it to date human cells, and what they found was not uniform turnover. Most of the neurons in your cerebral cortex are as old as you are. They were made around the time you were born and they were never replaced. Heart muscle turns over slowly — roughly one percent a year in your twenties, less than half that by your seventies — so most of your heart, too, is original equipment. The proteins in the lens of your eye were laid down before you could see properly and are never renewed, which is a large part of why eyes eventually cloud. Tooth enamel has no living cells in it at all; what you erupted with is what you have.

So you are not a river. You are a hybrid: an Ise shrine with a few original planks left in. And the distribution is not random. The parts that get replaced are the parts that do the wearing — the surfaces that touch the world, the cells that get abraded and digested and sloughed. The parts that persist are the parts that hold the record. The lens keeps its proteins because it needs perfect optical order and cannot afford to rebuild. The cortex keeps its neurons because whatever you are is written into their connections, and you cannot re-thatch a memory.

There is something almost unbearable in that. The maintenance strategy of a human being is to continuously replace everything except the thing that would be lost by replacing it. Which means the irreplaceable part is exactly the part that has to survive without renewal, aging in place, for eighty years, while the rest of the building is rebuilt around it sixty times.

---

I want to resist the tidy conclusion here, because the tidy conclusion is that objects are illusions and only processes are real, and that's a little too cheap, and also it lets a certain kind of vandalism off the hook.

Rebuilding is not innocent. Every act of remaking is an opportunity to change something quietly and then claim you didn't. Traditions that advertise their timelessness are very often the most recently invented, and the advertisement is doing political work. The empty lot can be a calendar, or it can be an alibi.

And there's the plain fact that some things really are only their matter. Nobody thinks a rebuilt Vermeer is a Vermeer. The distinction isn't between old and new. It's between things whose identity is a *pattern that can be re-performed* and things whose identity is a *trace that cannot*. Most of the confusion in arguments about restoration, and covers, and remakes, and revivals comes from people applying the logic of one to the other.

What I take from the gravel, in the end, is a shift in the question. The instinct, when you love something, is to ask how to keep it. Wrap it, climate-control it, insure it, put it behind glass. And that instinct is right for traces and wrong for almost everything else — wrong for crafts, wrong for languages, wrong for institutions, wrong for a body of scientific results that only stays alive if somebody actually reruns the experiment, wrong for a friendship, wrong for the ability to play a piece of music. For all of those, the question isn't *how do I keep this* but *who is going to know how to make it again, and have I given them enough time to learn.* Preservation, for living things, is a scheduling problem. You have to build the twenty years into the thing.

There are people in Mie Prefecture who were apprentices in 2013. They are in their late thirties and forties now. In 2033 they should be the ones directing the work, and there should be twenty-year-olds standing beside them watching, badly, learning the feel of a joint that no document describes. And when it's finished, the shrine will move one plot to the left, and the gravel will be raked, and the little hut will go up in the middle of it with the post inside, and the emptiness will start counting again.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an open creative invitation. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, something I can write about with depth and specificity rather than generic filler. Let me think about what would actually make good writing here.

Options:
- An essay on something concrete and surprising — the history of a specific object, a scientific idea, a place
- Something about language, translation, untranslatability
- Something about maps, borders, the Aral Sea
- Something about the way information decays — the story of the Antikythera mechanism, or lost libraries
- Something about attention and noticing
- A piece about the humble things: the history of the pencil, the shipping container, the standardized screw thread
- Something about time and deep time — the Oklo natural nuclear reactor, the nuclear waste warning problem (10,000 year markers)

I like the nuclear waste warning problem — "This place is not a place of honor." It's genuinely fascinating, has real texture, connects to language, deep time, the limits of communication, and it's a subject I find compelling. But it's somewhat well-trodden in essay circles.

Another: the problem of the color blue in ancient languages, Homer's wine-dark sea, the Himba color perception studies. Also somewhat trodden.

Patterson: trying to date the Earth using lead isotopes in meteorites, had to invent the clean room, discovered industrial lead contamination everywhere, then fought the leaded gasoline industry, won, and the lead in human blood dropped by 80%. And he died... he died in 1995. And the irony that he saved more lives than almost anyone while being obscure. That's a great story but it's also been popularized by Cosmos.
